background.definition: In 2005, the World Health Organization (WHO) adopted the following definition: "Drowning is the process of experiencing respiratory impairment from submersion/immersion in liquid".

list.listitem: There is approximately one case of drowning per 100,000 persons per year in the United States.

Between 2005 and 2009, there were 3880 unintentional fatal drownings in the United States per year, averaging over 10 per day, and 5789 non-fatal near-drownings treated in US hospital emergency departments.
The highest rates are among children age 4 years or younger.

Overall, drowning is the 3rd leading cause of death from unintentional injury around the world. It is the most common cause of death in children 1 to 4 years and second most common cause due to unintentional injury in older children.

"Dry" drowning is due to laryngospasm, followed by hypoxia and then loss of consciousness. There is little or no fluid in the lungs. It accounts for 10% to 20% of deaths. "Wet" drowning is due to aspiration of water into the lungs and dilution and washout of pulmonary surfactant.
Patients with seizure disorder are at greatly increased risk of drowning, with a standardized incidence ratio for drowning of 18.7 (95% CI, 15–23) in a systematic review.
Other risk factors include male sex, young age, alcohol use, swimming in lakes and rivers rather than pools, and lack of supervision or fencing.
In a retrospective review of 1243 drowning deaths, 82% were male and most events occurred in open water in warm temperatures.
The pathophysiology of drowning is thought to initially involve breath-holding, followed by an involuntary gasp or breath leading to aspiration of water into the hypopharynx.
This triggers laryngospasm. In some cases (dry drowning), little water is aspirated, but in most patients water is aspirated into the lungs after the laryngospasm releases.
In both cases, the result is increasing hypoxemia, and eventually cerebral hypoxia, acidosis, and cardiac dysrhythmias.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Recreational boating wearing a life vest

list.listitem: Parental vigilance is essential during toddler bathing and swimming. Children and adults should be taught to swim, and should not swim after ingesting alcohol. Ideally, swim in places with a lifeguard present.C
A Cochrane review found that pool fences significantly reduce the risk of drowning (OR 0.27; 95% CI, 0.16–0.47). B
Boaters should use personal flotation devices.C
Children should be supervised when in or near water, including bathtubs. Parental education programs may help improve alertness and behavioral outcomes, although effect on drowning is uncertain.C

Differential.Differential_Features: General quadriplegia with little respiratory distress
History of seizure disorder or seizure observed

list.listitem: Diagnosis of drowning and near-drowning involves the observation of a constellation of signs of symptoms of a victim of a possible submersion injury. Signs include a swimmer flailing his/her arms, displaying irregular swimming motions, lying motionless and face down in the water, and motionless with only the head showing above water with the mouth open.
Other signs include abdominal distension and vomiting, cyanosis, cough with pink/frothy sputum, decreased or absent level of consciousness, respiratory distress or apnea, weak or absent pulses.
Order pulse oximetry, arterial blood gasses, chest x-ray.
Consider cervical spine imaging if warranted by injuries or mechanism (i.e., a fall from a height). Only 0.5% of drownings involve cervical spine injury.
Order a CBC, glucose, coagulation studies, CPK, urinalysis, urine drug screen and electrolytes.
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) values were found to be the most useful predictors of outcome in one study of 51 patients treated for drowning.

A retrospective review of 39 saltwater near-drowning victims (mean age 14 years) found the following frequencies of electrolyte abnormalities: hypobicarbonatemia (71%), hyperchloremia (38%); high-anion gap (59%), hypernatremia (31%) and hypokalemia (21%).
Perform an ECG and order cardiac monitoring.
A clinical decision rule has been developed to predict the prognosis of children who have experienced near drowning ().

In the field, provide rescue ventilation (drowning victims may have gasping breaths or apnea but still have a heartbeat). Use the traditional ABC sequence (Airway—Breathing—Circulation) for drowning victims rather than the now recommended CAB sequence for non-drowning cardiac arrest. This is to re-expand water-filled alveoli first. Do not use abdominal thrusts, this may increase the likelihood of regurgitation and aspiration or airway obstruction.
Measure vital signs, watching specifically for hypothermia; tachycardia or bradycardia; tachypnea, agonal or absent respirations; and hypotension.
Perform a neurologic examination including the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS). Prognosis and treatment is different for those with a GCS greater or equal to 13 and those with a score less than 13.

Provide active cardiopulmonary resuscitation, in the order airway - breathing - circulation, remembering that special circumstances may be present including head or cervical spine trauma; hypothermia; drug or alcohol intoxication; and other comorbidity (epilepsy, diabetes).C
Provide supportive care including supplemental oxygen, and mechanical ventilation if needed. Supranormal levels of PEEP may be required. C
Patients may develop acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) with significant aspirations. B
Most victims improve within 24 hours; only a minority require hospitalization for longer than 24 hours.B

Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended as routine practice. Monitor for signs of pneumonia and initiate antibiotics if they develop. Pneumonia is most likely in when submersion is in polluted or dirty water, and is very unlikely in swimming pool drownings.
Microorganisms retrieved from seawater immersion were either part of the human oropharyngeal flora or Enterobacteriaceae and generally displayed low rate of antimicrobial resistance.
Drowning associated pneumonia may be caused by multi-drug resistant bacteria, and the spectrum of bacteria is similar to that in the body of water.
Bronchodilators are recommended for bronchospasm, but corticosteroids are not routinely recommended, as there is no clear evidence that they prevent pulmonary injury.
Treatment is based on neurologic and cardiovascular examination on arrival to the ED. Use the order airway - breathing - circulation to first re-expand water-filled alveoli.
AHA/AAP guidelines (2024) recommend that resuscitation begin with in-water rescue breathing if necessary, and continue with chest compressions once on dry land or a boat.
A proposed grading system from one to six classifies patients according to clinical findings (see ).
If the GCS is 13 or higher, provide supplemental oxygen to keep oxygen saturation >95% and observe for 4 to 6 hours; admit if pulmonary status does not improve.

If the GCS is less than 13, provide supplemental oxygen and mechanical ventilation if necessary (respiratory failure or impending failure), warmed IV fluids, and warming devices. Patients may need supranormal levels of PEEP if ventilation is required. Patients should generally be kept on mechanical ventilation, once initiated, for at least 24 hours.
Evaluate carefully for associated injuries, especially head injury, cervical spine injury, fractures, hypothermia. Consider possibility of new onset seizure disorder.
Induced hypothermia may be neuroprotective, and good outcomes have been reported in small case series.
Very good outcomes have been achieved following cold water drownings using extracorporeal membrane oxygenation.

For resuscitation by lifeguards, successful ventilations with one of three supraglotic airways (Intersurgical® i-gel; Protatex® Soft Seal or Ambu® AuraOnce) was found to be feasible when applied to manikins.

A study using mannequins compared in water resuscitation on a surfboard using a pocket mask with resuscitation not using in water breathing. In water resuscitation on the board resulted in shorter reoxygenation time but it took longer to get the "victim" to shore.

Continue basic life support unless signs of life re-appear, ALS is available, or rescuer exhaustion. Continue advanced life until the patient has been rewarmed (if hypothermic) and asystole persists for more than 20 minutes.

In children with drowning-induced cardiac arrest, favorable neurological outcomes were rare (3.5%) and nearly absent after >33 minutes of out-of-hospital CPR (0.3%). CPR beyond 33 minutes had a high positive predictive value (0.98) for poor neurological outcomes, though outcome prediction remains challenging.
Prognosis is poor if CPR or artificial ventilation is required, and especially if asystole is the cardiac arrest rhythm.B

Outcome is worse with increasing duration of submersion. The likelihood of death or severe neurologic impairment is 10% if ≤5 minutes, 56% if 6 to 10 minutes, 88% if 11 to 25 minutes, and nearly 100% if >25 minutes. B
There are only anecdotal reports of complete neurologic recovery after prolonged warm water submersion. C
See for prognosis by clinical findings.B

A risk score was developed in 103 drowning cardiac arrest patients to predict 28 day mortality. Predictors included a duration of CPR longer than 20 minutes, ICU admission temperature < 34C, lactate > 7 mmol/L and requiring invasive mechanical ventilation. The risk score had an AUC of 0.91 but requires prospective validation.
Probability of neurologically intact survival to discharge from the hos[ital is 90% if 0 to < 5 minutes, 44% if 5 to < 10 minutest, 12% if 10 to < 25 minutes, and 0.1% if > 25 minutes.

Risk factors for clinically important drowning-associated lung injury (ciDALI) in children include age >5 years (aOR 2.4), submersion >5 minutes (aOR 6.0), scene resuscitation (aOR 3.3), and abnormal ED findings (mentation aOR 6.4, lung auscultation OR 3.9).
